content: Co-sleeping, also referred to as the family bed, is a practice where infants and young children sleep in the same bed as one or both parents. This practice is common in many parts of the world outside of North America, Europe, and Australia. In some cases, children may join their parents in bed during the night. A 2006 study conducted in India found that 93% of children aged 3 to 10 co-slept with their parents. Historically, co-sleeping was a widespread practice globally until the 19th century, when the concept of giving children their own rooms and cribs became more prevalent. In many cultures, co-sleeping serves a practical purpose, such as keeping the child warm during the night. In recent years, co-sleeping has been reintroduced into Western culture, particularly by advocates of attachment parenting. For example, a 2006 study in Kentucky, USA, reported that 15% of infants and toddlers aged 2 weeks to 2 years co-slept with their parents. Proponents of co-sleeping argue that it offers several benefits, including saving infants' lives (especially when combined with breastfeeding), fostering parent-child bonding, allowing parents to get more sleep, facilitating breastfeeding, and potentially reducing the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Older infants can breastfeed during the night without fully waking their mothers. However, opponents of co-sleeping raise concerns about its potential risks. They argue that co-sleeping can be stressful and dangerous for the baby, particularly due to modern bedding, which may not be safe for this practice. Critics point to evidence suggesting that co-sleeping may increase the risk of SIDS. They also highlight the possibility of accidental smothering by the parent or fostering an unhealthy dependence of the child on the parent. Additionally, opponents note that co-sleeping may interfere with the parents' relationship, reducing opportunities for communication and sexual intimacy at bedtime. Some advice suggests that co-sleeping often ends naturally after a year or two if the child is not forced to continue. Children may choose their own sleeping arrangements, sometimes opting for surfaces that adults might find uncomfortable. Factors such as hot weather and weaning can encourage this natural separation. The safety and health implications of co-sleeping are a topic of debate among healthcare professionals. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) advises against co-sleeping, but many pediatricians, breastfeeding advocates, and other experts have criticized the CPSC's recommendations. There are potential health advantages to co-sleeping. One study found that mothers who co-slept and breastfed got more sleep compared to other arrangements. It has been suggested that co-sleeping evolved over millions of years and that it alters the infant's sleep patterns and increases maternal monitoring of the baby. This practice may also provide insights into unconventional ways to reduce the risk of SIDS. Stress hormones, such as cortisol, are lower in mothers and babies who co-sleep, which is important for the baby's healthy growth. Animal studies have shown that infants who remain close to their mothers exhibit higher levels of growth hormones and enzymes essential for brain and heart development. Co-sleeping infants also demonstrate more stable physiological parameters, such as body temperature, heart rhythms, and fewer prolonged pauses in breathing, compared to infants who sleep alone. Furthermore, co-sleeping has been associated with long-term emotional health benefits. Follow-up studies have shown that children who co-slept with their parents were happier, less anxious, had higher self-esteem, were less likely to fear sleep, exhibited fewer behavioral problems, were more comfortable with intimacy, and were generally more independent as adults. Despite its potential benefits, co-sleeping carries risks, particularly when a parent smokes. Other risk factors include parental drug or alcohol use, extreme obesity, and unsafe sleeping surfaces such as waterbeds or couches. To reduce risks, it is recommended that babies sleep on their backs, not their stomachs, and that heavy bedding, such as quilts and pillows, be avoided. Babies should not sleep next to young children under nine months of age, and they should never be left unattended in an adult bed. There is also a risk of the baby falling onto a hard floor. Several products are available to facilitate safer co-sleeping. These include bassinets that attach to the side of an adult bed with barriers on three sides, bed-top co-sleeping products designed to prevent the baby from rolling off the bed, side rails for adult beds, and infant enclosures placed directly in the adult bed. The prevalence of co-sleeping varies. A study in Northeast England found that 65% of parents had shared a bed with their child at some point, with 95% of these parents doing so with both partners present. Some parents found bed-sharing effective but were discreet about the practice due to fear of disapproval from healthcare professionals and relatives. Additionally, a National Center for Health Statistics survey conducted between 1991 and 1999 found that 25% of American families always or almost always co-slept with their baby, 42% did so sometimes, and 32% never co-slept.
